keyVerseText: And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains : he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. an Hachmonite: or, son of Hachmoni
rootMeaning: The name יָשׇׁבְעָם (Yâshobʻâm) derives from the Hebrew roots שׁוּב (shûwb), meaning 'to return' or 'to bring back,' and עַם ('am), meaning 'people.' Literally, it conveys the idea that 'the people will return.' This etymology enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing a dynamic of restoration and communal return, suggesting a hopeful or redemptive movement rather than a static identity.
usageInScripture: The word יָשׇׁבְעָם occurs three times in Scripture, consistently referring to a proper name for one or more Israelite individuals, specifically mighty warriors associated with King David. The top translations—'had Jashobeam,' 'and Jashobeam,' and 'was Jashobeam'—show that the name is used primarily as a marker of identity within lists or narratives of David's warriors, underscoring the personal valor and leadership embodied by these figures.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יָשׇׁבְעָם as 'the people will return' invites reflection on God's faithfulness to restore His people, a theme central to biblical theology. The name's association with David's mighty warriors highlights how God raises leaders who embody strength and deliverance for His covenant community. This restoration motif points forward to the ultimate return and reconciliation found in Christ, who gathers His people and leads them into spiritual victory. Thus, the name serves as a reminder that God's redemptive plan involves both individual faithfulness and communal restoration under His sovereign rule.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Chronicles 11:11 describes Jashobeam as an Hachmonite and chief captain who heroically slew three hundred men at once. The use of יָשׇׁבְעָם here not only identifies this mighty warrior but also subtly connects his personal valor to the broader theme of God's people returning and being restored through faithful leadership. His role as a leader among David's warriors exemplifies how God equips His servants to secure victory and bring about the restoration of His people.
